newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court upholds BA Gulf hostages compensation.
newsitem.headline: French court upholds BA Gulf hostages compensation.

text.p: A French appeals court upheld a lower court ruling on Tuesday ordering British Airways to compensate 61 Gulf War hostages for landing them in Iraqi hands in occupied Kuwait, justice sources said.

The 61 French nationals and foreign residents of France were among 364 people aboard a BA flight from London which landed at Kuwait airport on August 2, 1990 -- four hours after Iraqi invaders entered the emirate.

The British airline had appealed against last year's order to pay the hostages 400,000 to 600,000 francs ($80,000 to $120,000) each in damages, according to the time they spent in captivity by Iraqi forces -- a total of 26 million francs ($5.2 million).
The Paris appeals court confirmed the compensation for all but five of the 61 hostages, for whom it ordered slightly lower compensation for loss of luggage, the sources said.
"In a reckless manner and for no justified reason, British Airways laid its passengers open to a risk of war," the ruling said.
It said that the situation on August 1, 1990, was particularly alarming given that peace talks had failed and that the foreign press had reported Iraqi troop movements.
Lawyers for the airline said they would make a new appeal, this time to the Supreme Court.
The plaintiffs charged BA had committed a "severe error" and demanded compensation for the mental anguish they suffered.

British Airways argued it had no way of knowing that the invasion was under way. It said the hostages had already been paid compensation of around 30,000 francs ($6,000) each out of a French state fund set up for victims of terrorist or similar attacks.
Iraqi soldiers seized the Boeing 747, and its passengers were held hostage for up to three months, some being used as human shields against allied bombing of strategic Iraqi sites.
BA denies the plaintiffs' allegation that the flight landed at Kuwait to drop off 15 undercover British Special Air Service Regiment (SAS) soldiers who boarded at the last minute.
The ruling by the appeals court made no mention of this allegation.

"The ruling recognises the calvary endured in Iraq for three months and because of British Airways which used us like sandbags. Civil aviation was used for military purposes," Paul Merlet, one of the 61 passengers, told reporters.
The French government had joined the ex-hostages in demanding that the airline reimburse its guarantee fund and pay additional damages.
